modules.title: SD-WAN: members, health checks, rules and troubleshooting
objectives: Name the SD-WAN building blocks and how traffic flows through them
Design performance SLAs with sensible servers, thresholds and timers
Choose the right rule strategy for each application and explain the choice to a customer
Explain why a rule doesn't match, using the FIB checks and the implicit rule
Troubleshoot steering with the guide's command map, from health check to policy route to session
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: SD-WAN overview and components (pp. 1155–1158), quick start (pp. 1159–1169)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: members and zones (pp. 1170–1177), performance SLA (pp. 1193–1199)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: SD-WAN rules, strategies and implicit rule (pp. 1254–1274), troubleshooting (pp. 1776–1778)

units.title: The building blocks
units.body:
SD-WAN is built into FortiOS. Five pieces make it work (p. 1158):

1. **Members:** the interfaces that carry traffic: physical ports, VLANs, LAGs, IPsec tunnels and more (p. 1170). Each member can have a **cost** (lower is preferred, used by the Lowest Cost strategy) and a gateway.
2. **Zones:** groups of members. Members you don't place go into the default zone **virtual-wan-link**. A common design is an **Underlay** zone (ISP links) and an **Overlay** zone (IPsec to the hub) (pp. 1173–1174).
3. **Performance SLAs (health checks):** probes that measure each member's latency, jitter and packet loss, and detect dead links.
4. **SD-WAN rules (services):** which traffic goes where, with a **strategy**.
5. **The implicit rule:** what happens to traffic no rule matched.

## Zones are what policies and routes see

Firewall policies use **zones** as source or destination, not individual members; the rules hold the intelligence about which member to use (pp. 1162, 1175). A static route can point to a zone with `set sdwan-zone`, and a route via an SD-WAN zone has **administrative distance 1** by default (pp. 1161, 1177).

## The quick-start design

Fortinet's quick start goes **underlay → overlay → routing → security → SD-WAN** (pp. 1159–1162): get the ISP links up, build IPsec overlays, add routing (often BGP over the overlays), write the security policies, then add SD-WAN members, health checks and rules.

:::recall
Q: Where do you reference SD-WAN in a firewall policy: the member or the zone?
A: The zone. Rules then decide which member inside it is used.
:::

units.title: Performance SLAs that tell the truth
units.body:
A health check is a **probe mode, protocol and server** (p. 1194).

- **Mode:** active probes, passive (measured from real sessions through the policies), or prefer-passive.
- **Protocols:** ping, TCP echo, UDP echo, HTTP, HTTPS, TWAMP, DNS (p. 1195). Predefined profiles exist for DNS, FortiGuard, Gmail, Google Search and Office 365.
- **Servers:** you can give two; **both must fail** for the check to fail, so one dead server doesn't take a link down. A server can be used in **only one** SLA (p. 1198). Probe a server on the path the application uses, not a random public site.

## Targets and timers (p. 1198)

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| Latency threshold | 5 ms |
| Jitter threshold | 5 ms |
| Packet loss threshold | 0 % |
| Check interval | 500 ms |
| Failures before inactive (`failtime`) | 5 |
| Restore link after (`recoverytime`) | 5 |

Those defaults are strict. Set targets from the application's real needs, a little inside the limit: if voice needs under 150 ms, target around 135 ms. Too tight means traffic flaps between links; too loose and users suffer before SD-WAN reacts.

## Two independent states (p. 1199)

- **Dead / Alive:** basic reachability. Dead members aren't used.
- **In-SLA / Out-of-SLA:** within the thresholds or not. A link can be Alive and Out-of-SLA.

**Lowest Cost (SLA)** prefers Alive + In-SLA members. **Manual** and **Best Quality** only look at Dead/Alive. With `update-static-route enable`, a dead member's static routes are withdrawn, so routing stops using it too (pp. 1169, 1199).

:::pitfall
Probing 8.8.8.8 to steer traffic to Azure tells you about Google, not Azure. Match the probe to the destination the rule serves.
:::

units.title: Rules and strategies
units.body:
A rule matches traffic (source, destination, protocol, ports, users, **Internet Service Database** entries, applications, DSCP) and picks an outgoing member by **strategy** (pp. 1256–1262). Members listed first in a rule are preferred, unless the strategy reorders them (p. 1260).

| Strategy | CLI | Decides by | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Manual | manual | The order you set | Fixed preference, e.g. backup link only on failure |
| Best Quality | priority | The best value of one metric (link-cost-factor: latency, jitter, loss, bandwidth…) | Real-time apps that need the best link right now |
| Lowest Cost (SLA) | sla | Cheapest member that meets the SLA targets | Business apps: use the cheap link while it's good enough |
| Maximize Bandwidth (SLA) | load-balance | Spreads across all members meeting SLA | Bulk traffic, backups |

**Automatic** also exists, without SLA logic (p. 1261).

## Why didn't my rule match?

By default an SD-WAN rule is only used when the **FIB best match for the destination is an SD-WAN member**, and a member is only selected if it **has a valid route** to the destination (p. 1262). So a more specific static route out a non-SD-WAN interface bypasses the rule entirely. Check routing before blaming the rule.

Rules are evaluated in order like policy routes. **Policy routes are checked before SD-WAN rules**, which is easy to forget during a migration.

## The implicit rule (p. 1269)

No rule matched → the **implicit rule**: the default route via the SD-WAN zone has every active member as an **ECMP** path, balanced by `load-balance-mode`: **source-ip-based (default)**, weight-based, source-dest-ip-based, measured-volume-based.

:::recall
Q: A customer wants voice on the best link at every moment, and SaaS on the cheap broadband unless it's bad. Which strategies?
A: Best Quality for voice; Lowest Cost (SLA) for SaaS.
:::

:::delta
Application-based rules need *Application Detection Based SD-WAN* enabled in Feature Visibility (p. 1259). ISDB entries are usually the safer match for SaaS, because the destination is known from the first packet.
:::

units.title: Troubleshooting with the guide's command map
units.body:
The troubleshooting chapter gives a progression (pp. 1776–1777). Follow it in order:

1. **Health:** `diagnose sys sdwan health-check` (state, loss, latency, jitter, `sla_map`), `diagnose sys link-monitor status`, `diagnose sys sdwan member`, `diagnose sys sdwan zone`.
2. **Rule decision:** `diagnose sys sdwan service4` (which members the rule selected and why), then the installed result with `diagnose firewall proute list` and `diagnose ip proute match`.
3. **Sessions and packets:** `diagnose sys session filter` + `list`, then `diagnose debug flow` with the sniffer.
4. **Overlays:** `diagnose vpn ike gateway list` and `diagnose vpn tunnel list`.
5. **Routing:** `get router info routing-table all`, `get router info kernel`, `diagnose ip route list` (RIB vs FIB).

## Common failure patterns (pp. 1777–1778)

| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| SLA healthy but traffic uses the wrong member | `service4`, then `proute list` / `ip proute match` |
| SLA flapping | `diagnose sys link-monitor interface <if>`, `diagnose test application lnkmtd 2` |
| Session exists but return traffic missing | session list + sniffer; check the return path's tunnel and route |
| Tunnel up but member not selected | health-check association and SLA state: `health-check` + `vpn tunnel list` |
| Routing table looks right, forwarding wrong | Compare RIB and FIB: `routing-table all`, `router info kernel`, `ip route list` |

:::pitfall
Existing sessions keep their route. After you change a rule, old sessions may still use the old member until they end or you clear them in a window.
:::

:::ps

scenarios.title: "SD-WAN isn't working, Teams is bad again"
scenarios.situation: A retail customer with 40 branches complains Teams calls are choppy at several stores, "even though we paid for SD-WAN".
scenarios.ask: How do you approach it, technically and with the customer?
right_thinking: Ask what 'bad' means: which stores, when, symptoms
Check whether a rule matches Teams at all, and with which strategy
Check the health check: probing the right destination? realistic targets?
Use data from the FortiGates to show the link quality per store
scenarios.what: A data-backed diagnosis and a rule/SLA change for real-time traffic.
scenarios.why: SD-WAN only steers as well as its rules and probes are designed.
how: service4 and session list: does Teams hit a rule or the implicit rule?
health-check: loss/jitter on each member at those stores
Add or fix an ISDB-based Teams rule with Best Quality on jitter or loss
Pilot in two stores, measure, then roll out
scenarios.model_answer: First I'd make "bad" specific: which stores, what times, and what users see. Then I'd look at one affected FortiGate. Often Teams isn't matched by any rule and falls into the implicit rule, which load-balances by source IP without looking at quality. I'd also check the health check: if it probes a generic site with default 5 ms targets, the data isn't meaningful. The fix is a Teams rule using the Internet Service Database with Best Quality on jitter or packet loss, and a probe on a relevant destination with realistic thresholds. I'd pilot it in two stores, show the customer before-and-after numbers, then roll it out with FortiManager.
could_have_added: Check whether the issue is the store Wi-Fi, not the WAN
scenarios.best_way: Make 'bad' specific, check whether Teams even hits a rule, fix the rule and probe, pilot, then show the numbers.

scenarios.situation: In a kickoff workshop the customer lists three traffic types: ERP to the data centre over the overlay, voice, and nightly backups to cloud storage. Two ISPs per site.
scenarios.ask: Propose a strategy per traffic type and explain it simply.
right_thinking: Map business need to strategy
ERP: reliable, cost-aware → Lowest Cost (SLA) over overlays
Voice: best link now → Best Quality on jitter/loss
Backups: throughput → Maximize Bandwidth
scenarios.what: A short strategy table the customer can sign off.
scenarios.why: Strategy choice is a business decision expressed in config.
how: One line per app: need → strategy → SLA numbers
Turn it into the test plan
scenarios.model_answer: ERP needs to be reliable and doesn't need the best link at every moment, so Lowest Cost (SLA): the preferred overlay while it meets the targets, failing over when it doesn't. Voice needs the best link right now, so Best Quality on jitter or packet loss. Backups need throughput and tolerate delay, so Maximize Bandwidth across links that meet SLA. I'd put that in a table with the thresholds you agree, and it becomes our test plan for go-live.
scenarios.best_way: ERP: Lowest Cost. Voice: Best Quality. Backups: Maximize Bandwidth. Agreed thresholds become the test plan.

interview.question: Explain how FortiGate SD-WAN decides which link a session uses.
interview.model_answer: "Members are grouped into zones, and health checks measure each member. When a new session arrives, policy routes are checked first, then SD-WAN rules in order. A rule only applies if routing points the destination at SD-WAN, and its strategy picks the member: manual order, best quality on a metric, lowest cost that meets the SLA, or maximize bandwidth. If no rule matches, the implicit rule load-balances with ECMP, by source IP by default."
interview.best_way: Policy routes, then SD-WAN rules with a strategy and health data, then the implicit ECMP rule.

interview.question: How would you design health checks for a SaaS application?
interview.model_answer: "Probe something on the application's path, ideally the SaaS provider's endpoint, with HTTP or HTTPS if ping is filtered, and two servers so one dead server doesn't fail the link. Set targets from what the app needs, slightly inside the limit, because the 5 ms defaults would flap on any real internet link. And keep failtime and recoverytime so it doesn't bounce."
interview.best_way: Probe the app's path with two servers, realistic targets, and damping timers.

interview.question: An SD-WAN rule doesn't match the traffic you expect. What do you check?
interview.framework: Routing → policy routes → rule match → commands
interview.model_answer: "First routing: by default a rule is only consulted if the FIB best match is an SD-WAN member, so a more specific route elsewhere bypasses it. Then policy routes, which come first. Then the rule's match criteria and order. diagnose sys sdwan service4 shows the rule's selection, diagnose firewall proute list the installed result, and diagnose ip proute match what a given packet would use."
interview.best_way: Routing first, then policy routes, then the rule. service4, proute list and proute match prove it.

interview.question: Tell me about a rollout you planned with a customer. How did you make sure it succeeded?
interview.testing: Delivery approach (bridge from your Netskope rollouts)
interview.model_answer: "[Use your Netskope rollout story: the account you took from below 50 % to 70 % utilisation.] Show the same pattern you'd use for SD-WAN: agree success criteria first, pilot with a small group, measure, adjust, then scale with the customer and partner, with a clear communication plan."
interview.best_way: Success criteria, pilot, measure, scale: the same pattern for SD-WAN.

interview.question: When would you choose Lowest Cost (SLA) over Best Quality?
interview.model_answer: "Lowest Cost uses the cheapest link as long as it meets the SLA targets, so it's for business apps that need good enough, like SaaS over broadband with MPLS as backup. Best Quality always picks the link with the best metric, so it's for real-time traffic like voice, where the best link right now matters more than cost."
interview.best_way: Lowest Cost for good-enough-and-cheap, Best Quality for real-time.

units.title: Two ways to look at TLS
units.body:
Most traffic is encrypted, so security profiles only see what SSL inspection lets them see. FortiOS ships four SSL/SSH inspection profiles (p. 3048): **certificate-inspection**, **deep-inspection** and **no-inspection** are read-only (clone them to change them), and **custom-deep-inspection** can be edited.

## Certificate inspection

The FortiGate only reads the handshake: up to the TLS layer, the **SNI and the server certificate**, not the content (p. 3052). That's enough for **web filtering by category**, application identification by name and blocking bad certificates, with no certificate deployment and less privacy impact. It **can't** see URLs paths, files, or malware inside the session.

When it blocks an HTTPS page, the user gets a block page signed by the FortiGate CA, so the browser warns unless the CA is trusted (pp. 3052–3054). The built-in certificate-inspection profile is read-only and **only listens on 443**; clone it to add ports such as 8443 (p. 3054).

## Deep (full) inspection

The FortiGate **impersonates the server to the client**: it terminates TLS, decrypts, inspects with AV, web filter, IPS, DLP and so on, re-encrypts and sends it on (p. 3056). It protects HTTPS and other TLS protocols (SMTPS, POP3S, IMAPS, FTPS).

Why it matters: malware downloaded over HTTPS and command-and-control channels are encrypted, so without deep inspection they "might get past your network's security measures" (p. 3055).

:::recall
Q: A customer wants category filtering only and no certificate rollout. Which profile?
A: Certificate inspection: it reads SNI and the server certificate, enough for categories.
:::

:::delta
Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) hides the SNI. The profile can allow or block ECH; with certificate inspection, ECH limits what you can classify (p. 3050).
:::

units.title: Rolling out deep inspection without warnings
units.body:
With deep inspection, the browser receives a certificate **re-signed by the FortiGate**. By default the profile uses **Fortinet_CA_SSL** (p. 3054). If clients don't trust that CA, every site shows a warning.

## Two CAs, one rule

- Server certificate **trusted** → FortiGate re-signs with **Fortinet_CA_SSL** (or your own CA).
- Server certificate **untrusted** → FortiGate re-signs with **Fortinet_CA_Untrusted**, so the user still sees a warning for a genuinely bad site.
- **Never import Fortinet_CA_Untrusted into browsers** (p. 3056). That would hide real attacks.

## Use the customer's PKI

In production, use a CA from the customer's own PKI rather than the factory CA (p. 4435): it's already trusted by managed devices and **can be revoked** if compromised. Microsoft's two-tier practice: an **offline Root CA** signs an **issuing sub-CA**, and the sub-CA signs the certificate the FortiGate uses for inspection (pp. 4435–4436).

## Distribute the CA

Download the CA from the profile (*Download* next to CA certificate) and install it in the **Trusted Root Certification Authorities** store; for domain PCs, push it with **Group Policy** (p. 3057). Plan non-Windows devices separately: macOS, mobiles (MDM), Linux servers, and apps with their own certificate stores (Firefox, Java, Python).

## Rollout plan

1. Pilot group and a pilot policy, with exemptions ready.
2. Distribute the CA before you enable inspection.
3. Enable deep inspection on the pilot policy; watch SSL logs and user reports.
4. Add exemptions for broken apps, then widen in phases.

:::pitfall
Users still see warnings after you imported Fortinet_CA_SSL? Check whether the site's real certificate is untrusted: then the warning is coming from Fortinet_CA_Untrusted, and it's correct (p. 3056).
:::

units.title: Exemptions, invalid certificates and protocol options
units.body:
## Exemptions (Full SSL only, pp. 3050–3051, 3057)

Exempt sessions from deep inspection by:

- **Reputable websites:** a FortiGuard allowlist of common trusted sites.
- **Web categories:** **Finance and Banking, Health and Wellness, and Personal Privacy** are exempt by default; they're also the categories most likely to involve privacy rules or pinned certificates.
- **Addresses:** IP, range, subnet, FQDN, wildcard FQDN, geography.
- Turn on **Log SSL exemptions** so you can prove what was exempted.

Typical exemptions: banking and health (privacy, law), apps with **certificate pinning** (they reject any re-signed certificate), OS and security-agent updates, and partner services that use client certificates.

## Invalid certificate actions (p. 3051)

With *Custom*: **expired → block**, **revoked → block**, **validation failed → block** (defaults); validation timed-out → allow (certificate inspection) or *Keep Untrusted & Allow* (deep inspection). Deep inspection actions: *Keep Untrusted & Allow*, *Block*, *Trust & Allow*. **SSL anomaly logging is on by default** (UTM log, SSL subtype).

## Other settings worth knowing

- **SNI check** (p. 3050): compare SNI with the certificate CN/SAN; *Strict* closes mismatches.
- **Inspect all ports**: in **flow mode deep inspection, all ports are scanned anyway**; in proxy mode only mapped ports unless *Inspect all ports* is on (p. 3052).
- **Minimum TLS version** per protocol with `min-allowed-ssl-version`, and `unsupported-ssl-version {allow | block}` (p. 3058).
- **HTTP/3 and DNS over QUIC**: inspect, bypass or block under Full SSL (p. 3050). Blocking QUIC makes browsers fall back to TCP/TLS, which you can inspect.

:::why
Q: Why exempt Finance and Banking by default?
A: Privacy and regulation, and banking sites and apps often break with re-signed certificates. Inspecting them adds risk and little security value.
:::

units.title: Inbound servers, offload and the consultant's checklist
units.body:
## Protecting an SSL server (pp. 3058–3059)

For inbound traffic to your own web server, there's no need to impersonate anyone: import the **server's own certificate and private key** into the FortiGate, create a profile with **Protecting SSL Server**, select the certificate, and use it on the inbound (VIP) policy. The FortiGate presents the real server certificate, decrypts and inspects (IPS, AV, WAF in proxy mode).

## Behind an external decryptor

If load balancers decrypt before and re-encrypt after the FortiGate (an "SSL offload sandwich"), enable `ssl-offloaded` in the protocol options so the FortiGate scans the plain text (p. 3059).

## Certificates on the FortiGate itself

Replace the self-signed admin certificate with a signed one: import the signed certificate and its CA under *System > Certificates*, then `set admin-server-cert <name>` under `config system global` (p. 4435). The same certificate can serve Agentless VPN.

## Consultant's checklist before go-live

- Legal/HR sign-off on what is decrypted and logged (privacy policy, works councils, local law).
- Which CA, issued by whom, revocation plan.
- Distribution to every device type, tested.
- Exemption list agreed, with an owner.
- Pilot, then phases; a rollback (switch the policy back to certificate inspection).
- Sizing: deep inspection costs CPU; check the model's SSL inspection throughput.

:::threat
Ransomware featured in 48 % of breaches in the 2026 DBIR, and most malware and command-and-control now hide inside TLS. Without deep inspection, AV and IPS see only encrypted bytes.
:::

scenarios.title: "Turn on SSL inspection for everyone on Monday"
scenarios.situation: The CISO of a 1,200-user company wants deep inspection on all internet traffic from Monday, after a phishing incident. Laptops are domain-joined; there are also Macs and unmanaged BYOD phones on the guest Wi-Fi.
scenarios.ask: How do you respond and plan it?
right_thinking: Support the goal: the incident is a real reason
A big-bang rollout breaks things and burns trust; propose a fast phased plan
CA distribution per device type, privacy sign-off, exemptions
BYOD: certificate inspection only, or no CA deployment
scenarios.what: A one-week phased plan with clear decisions for the CISO.
scenarios.why: Deep inspection done badly leads to it being switched off; done well it stays on.
how: Day 1: legal/HR sign-off, exemption list, CA from their PKI
Day 1–2: GPO for Windows, MDM for Macs; test
Day 2–3: pilot with IT and a business group
Day 4+: phases by department; BYOD stays on certificate inspection
scenarios.model_answer: I'd support the goal: after a phishing incident, inspecting HTTPS is the right move. But switching everyone on Monday will break apps and generate warnings, and the pressure will be to turn it off. I'd propose a fast phased plan instead: get privacy sign-off and agree exemptions like banking and health, issue the inspection certificate from their Microsoft PKI, push it by Group Policy to Windows and MDM to Macs, pilot with IT and one business team for two days, then roll out by department. Guest BYOD stays on certificate inspection because we can't install the CA there. They get protection within the week, and it sticks.
could_have_added: Show the SSL logs from the pilot as evidence of value
scenarios.best_way: Right goal; let's do it in a week, in phases: sign-off, CA via GPO and MDM, pilot, then departments. BYOD stays on certificate inspection.

scenarios.title: The app that broke
scenarios.situation: Day two of the pilot. Finance reports that their banking token software and a tax-authority portal client stopped working.
scenarios.ask: Diagnose and fix without weakening the whole policy.
right_thinking: Likely certificate pinning or client certificates
Find the destinations from logs, exempt narrowly
Log exemptions, document the owner
scenarios.what: Narrow exemptions with evidence.
scenarios.why: Broad exemptions defeat the purpose.
how: Check SSL/UTM logs for the user's sessions
scenarios.model_answer: These apps usually pin their certificate or use a client certificate, so a re-signed certificate breaks them. I'd find their destinations in the logs for that user, add narrow exemptions by FQDN or wildcard FQDN, not whole categories, and turn on exemption logging. Then retest with Finance and add the entries to the exemption register with an owner.
scenarios.best_way: Pinned apps: exempt their exact destinations, log it, and record who owns the exemption.

scenarios.title: What if legal says "no decryption of personal data"?
scenarios.situation: The customer's legal team says employees' personal browsing must not be decrypted.
scenarios.ask: What options do you give?
right_thinking: Respect the constraint; it's a requirement, not an obstacle
Exempt personal categories, decrypt business-relevant traffic
Certificate inspection for the rest still blocks bad categories
scenarios.what: A policy design that meets legal and security goals.
scenarios.why: The best design is one the customer can legally keep running.
scenarios.model_answer: That's a requirement we design around. Banking, health and personal privacy are already exempt by default, and we can exempt other personal categories legal names. We'd keep deep inspection where the risk is: uncategorized and newly registered domains, file downloads, and business apps. Everything else gets certificate inspection, which still blocks malicious categories without decrypting. Legal signs off the category list, and we log exemptions so audits are easy.
scenarios.best_way: Exempt personal categories, deep-inspect risky and business traffic, certificate-inspect the rest, with legal signing the list.

interview.question: What's the difference between certificate inspection and deep inspection?
interview.framework: What each sees → use case → trade-off
interview.model_answer: "Certificate inspection only reads the handshake, the SNI and the server certificate, so it's enough for category filtering with no certificate rollout. Deep inspection makes the FortiGate act as the server to the client: it decrypts, inspects with AV, IPS and web filter, and re-encrypts. It sees the content, but needs the CA trusted on devices, exemptions for pinned apps, and more CPU."
interview.best_way: Certificate inspection sees the handshake; deep inspection sees the content, at the cost of a CA rollout and CPU.

interview.question: After enabling deep inspection, users get certificate warnings. How do you troubleshoot?
interview.model_answer: "First, is it every site or some? Every site means the re-signing CA isn't trusted on that device, so I check how the CA was distributed, GPO, MDM, and app stores like Firefox. Some sites only: if their real certificate is untrusted, the FortiGate signs with Fortinet_CA_Untrusted on purpose, and that warning is correct. Never import that CA. Apps that fail without a warning are usually pinned, and need an exemption."
interview.best_way: All sites: CA not trusted on the device. Some sites: untrusted real certificate, working as designed. Apps: pinning, exempt them.

interview.question: How would you plan a deep-inspection rollout for an enterprise?
interview.testing: Delivery planning (I did this at Netskope)
interview.model_answer: "I've done this with customers at Netskope, rolling out SSL deep inspection with the CA pushed by Group Policy. The plan: privacy and legal sign-off and an exemption list, an inspection certificate from their PKI, distribution per device type, a pilot group, then phases by department with a rollback to certificate inspection. I track broken apps and add narrow exemptions as we go."
interview.best_way: Sign-off, CA from their PKI pushed by GPO and MDM, pilot, phases, narrow exemptions. I did this at Netskope.

interview.question: How do you inspect HTTPS going to a customer's own web server?
interview.model_answer: "With a Protecting SSL Server profile: import the server's certificate and private key into the FortiGate and use the profile on the inbound VIP policy. The FortiGate presents the real certificate, decrypts and inspects with IPS, and WAF in proxy mode. You don't use the outbound deep-inspection CA, because internet clients wouldn't trust it."
interview.best_way: Import the server's own certificate and key and use Protecting SSL Server on the inbound policy.

interview.question: How do you handle a customer who wants something done fast that you think is risky?
interview.framework: Agree goal → risk → faster safe path → decision in writing
interview.model_answer: "I agree with the goal first, then show the risk in their terms, and offer a path that's nearly as fast but safe. For example, a CISO who wants deep inspection for everyone on Monday: I'd propose a one-week phased rollout that gets them protection quickly without breaking apps. If they still want the risky route, I make sure the decision and risk are written down."
interview.best_way: Agree the goal, show the risk, offer a fast safe path, and get decisions in writing.

objectives: Choose flow or proxy inspection for a policy and justify it

sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: inspection modes (pp. 2481–2483), GenAI protection (p. 2500)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: antivirus (pp. 2522–2524), web filter (pp. 2598–2603), DNS filter (pp. 2693–2694)

units.title: Flow or proxy
units.body:
Each firewall policy has an inspection mode (p. 2481).

**Flow (the default, and recommended):** traffic isn't buffered. Content is inspected packet by packet, holding only the **last packet** until there's a verdict; if a threat is found, a **reset** is sent. All flow modules run in **one pass** with pattern matching that CP8/CP9 content processors accelerate. Lower resource use.

**Proxy:** the FortiGate **buffers the whole file, email or page**, inspects it, then releases it or replaces it with a **replacement message**. Client comforting trickles data so users don't time out (pp. 2481–2482).

Proxy-only capabilities include **video filter, inline CASB, WAF, content disarm and reconstruction (CDR), web quota, inline sandbox scanning**, and features that are only proxy-based such as **explicit web proxy, ZTNA and SSL offloading** (p. 2482). Most proxy features aren't supported on 2 GB RAM models.

Use flow unless you need a proxy feature, and keep the same mode across policies where you can: mixing modes costs performance (p. 2482). To configure profiles in a policy from the CLI, `set utm-status enable` first.

:::recall
Q: A customer needs Content Disarm and Reconstruction on email attachments. Which mode?
A: Proxy. CDR is a proxy-only feature.
:::

:::tip
Profiles have a *Feature set* (flow-based or proxy-based) so the GUI only shows the options that apply to that mode.
:::

units.title: Antivirus, web filter and DNS filter
units.body:
## Antivirus (pp. 2522–2524)

Signatures and engines are updated by **FortiGuard Antivirus** (subscription). New AV profiles default to **flow-based**. It can send suspicious files to **FortiSandbox** and block connections to botnet servers. FortiGuard only downloads AV definitions when **at least one policy uses an AV profile**. In flow mode, oversized files default to **pass**: tune `oversize-limit` deliberately.

## Web filter (pp. 2598–2603)

Checks happen in this order:

1. **URL filter** (your static allow/block/exempt list)
2. **FortiGuard web filtering** (categories)
3. **Web content filter** (words and patterns)
4. **Web script filter**
5. **Antivirus scanning**

FortiGuard category actions: **Allow, Monitor** (permit and log), **Block** (replacement message), **Warning** (user may continue), **Authenticate** (log in first). An *exempt* URL filter entry skips the later checks, so use it sparingly.

Preloaded profiles: `default`, `monitor-all`, `wifi-default`. A good first step with a new customer is **monitor** on everything for a week to learn what's used.

## DNS filter (pp. 2693–2694)

Blocks at name resolution, before any connection exists: **FortiGuard domain rating**, **botnet C&C domain blocking**, external dynamic categories, a local domain list, and an external IP block list for resolved addresses. In flow policies the IPS engine handles it; in proxy mode the DNS proxy does. It talks to the FortiGuard secure DNS servers over **anycast** by default.

:::why
Q: Why put DNS filter alongside web filter?
A: It blocks malicious and C&C domains for any application, not just web browsers, and before a connection is made. Web filter then handles full URLs on HTTP/HTTPS.
:::

units.title: Application control and IPS
units.body:
## Application control (pp. 2741–2744)

Uses IPS protocol decoders to identify applications. Preloaded sensors: `default` (monitor all), `wifi-default`, `block-high-risk`. Actions per category: **monitor, allow, block, quarantine**, plus **application and filter overrides** for exceptions.

**Which signature wins** when traffic matches several (p. 2743):

1. Entries (segments) are considered **in order**.
2. **Custom signatures beat FortiGuard** signatures.
3. Then signature weight and specificity (more specific apps beat broad protocols), visibility, pattern counts, and finally the higher (newer) ID.

Application control needs to see the traffic: with only certificate inspection, many apps inside TLS are identified by SNI; deep inspection adds sub-application control (for example, block uploads but allow viewing).

## IPS (pp. 2812–2818)

An **IPS sensor** is a set of **filters** (by severity, target, OS, protocol, application) and individual **signature entries**. Each signature has a default action; a filter's action **Default** applies it, or you override it (allow, monitor, block, reset, quarantine). Also: **botnet C&C** scanning (block or monitor outgoing connections to botnet IPs) and blocking malicious URLs for drive-by exploits.

Predefined sensors include `default` and `high_security` (Critical/High/Medium), `all_default`, `all_default_pass`, `protect_client`, `protect_email_server`, `protect_http_server` (p. 2813).

Fortinet recommends **tuning the sensor to what it protects**: only the signatures that match the services and devices behind the policy (p. 2812). A server-facing policy uses server signatures for that server's OS and applications; a user-facing outbound policy uses client signatures. Smaller, relevant sensors mean fewer false positives and better performance.

:::threat
IPS is a stop-gap while patches roll out. With exploitation the top initial access vector (31 %) and only 26 % of known-exploited vulnerabilities fully remediated in the 2026 DBIR, a tuned IPS sensor on exposed servers buys real time.
:::

units.title: GenAI, OT and operating the profiles
units.body:
## Controlling GenAI use (p. 2500)

Three layers, from coarse to fine:

- **Web filter:** the FortiGuard **Artificial Intelligence Technology** category to monitor or block AI sites.
- **Application control:** the **Generative AI** category, matching traffic patterns with deep packet inspection, beyond URLs.
- **DLP:** block prompts to LLM apps that contain specific keywords, to stop sensitive data leaving.

A sensible customer policy: allow the sanctioned AI tool, monitor the category to measure shadow AI, block uploads of sensitive data with DLP, and review the logs monthly.

## OT virtual patching (pp. 3034–3035)

With an OT license, **device detection** on the LAN interface and a **utm-status** policy, the FortiGate identifies OT/IoT devices and their vulnerabilities; a **virtual patching profile** blocks matching exploit traffic by severity (default action **block**). Only applies to OT devices.

## Profile groups (pp. 3125–3127)

Hidden in the GUI until enabled in the CLI. A group bundles AV, web filter, IPS, application control, SSL profile and more; a policy uses **either a group or individual profiles**, not both. Good for consistency across many policies or FortiGates.

## Operating them

- Start in **monitor**, review logs, then block with evidence.
- Licenses: AV, web filter, application control and IPS updates need FortiGuard subscriptions. Check the license page and `diagnose autoupdate versions` (engine and signature versions) before blaming a profile.
- Document exceptions (overrides, exempt URLs) with an owner and review date.

:::ps
Customers rarely ask "turn on IPS". They ask "can you stop this?" Translate the business risk into the smallest set of profiles that addresses it, and show the logs that prove it works.
:::

labs.title: Web filter and DNS filter for a new office
labs.goal: Block malicious and adult categories, monitor AI tools, and block botnet domains in DNS.

worked.config:
config webfilter profile
    edit "office-wf"
        set feature-set flow
        config ftgd-wf
            config filters
                edit 1
                    set category 26
                    set action block
                next
                edit 2
                    set category <AI-Technology-category-id>
                    set action monitor
                next
            end
        end
    next
end
config dnsfilter profile
    edit "office-dns"
        set block-botnet enable
        config ftgd-dns
            config filters
                edit 1
                    set category 26
                    set action block
                next
            end
        end
    next
end
config firewall policy
    edit 10
        set utm-status enable
        set ssl-ssh-profile "certificate-inspection"
        set webfilter-profile "office-wf"
        set dnsfilter-profile "office-dns"
    next
end
notes: Category 26 is Malicious Websites in FortiGuard; confirm IDs on your unit (the GUI shows names).
Look up the Artificial Intelligence Technology category ID in the GUI before using it.
Certificate inspection is enough for categories; deep inspection adds full URLs.

labs.title: A tuned IPS sensor for a DMZ web server
labs.goal: Protect a Linux Apache server with server-side signatures, block critical and high, and block botnet connections.

worked.config:
config ips sensor
    edit "dmz-web"
        set scan-botnet-connections block
        config entries
            edit 1
                set location server
                set os Linux
                set application Apache
                set severity high critical
                set action block
            next
            edit 2
                set location server
                set protocol HTTP
                set severity medium
                set action default
            next
        end
    next
end
config firewall policy
    edit 30
        set utm-status enable
        set ips-sensor "dmz-web"
    next
end
notes: Entry 1 matches signatures that apply to Linux AND Apache (filters are ANDed).
Entry 2 keeps each signature's own default action for medium severity.
Review IPS logs for false positives before tightening further.

faded.template:
config ips sensor
    edit "dmz-web"
        set {{scan-botnet-connections}} block
        config entries
            edit 1
                set location {{server}}
                set severity high critical
                set action {{block}}
            next
        end
    next
end

solo.prompt: Create IPS sensor users-out for outbound user traffic: client-side signatures, severity high and critical, action block, and monitor botnet connections.
solo.solution:
config ips sensor
    edit "users-out"
        set scan-botnet-connections monitor
        config entries
            edit 1
                set location client
                set severity high critical
                set action block
            next
        end
    next
end
solo.notes: protect_client is the predefined starting point for the same idea.

scenarios.title: "Stop people pasting customer data into ChatGPT"
scenarios.situation: A legal firm's managing partner asks you to stop staff pasting client documents into public AI tools, but they've licensed one approved AI assistant.
scenarios.ask: Design the controls and explain them to the partner.
right_thinking: Don't just block a category: they have a sanctioned tool
Layer: identify AI use, allow the sanctioned one, control data with DLP
Deep inspection is needed to see prompts and uploads
Measure and report shadow AI
scenarios.what: A layered GenAI policy with reporting.
scenarios.why: Blocking everything pushes users to personal devices; layered control keeps work visible.
how: Application control Generative AI category: allow the approved app, block or monitor others
DLP on prompts and uploads for client identifiers
Deep inspection on that policy, with privacy sign-off
scenarios.model_answer: I'd give them three layers. Application control on the Generative AI category: the approved assistant allowed, other AI tools blocked or at least monitored. DLP to stop prompts and uploads that contain client identifiers or document markers, which needs deep inspection on that policy, with the partners' sign-off. And a monthly report of who tried which tools, because shadow AI is a behaviour you manage, not just block. I did similar work at Netskope, getting a couple of accounts close to zero unsanctioned AI traffic with the same pattern: visibility first, then targeted control.
could_have_added: Combine with a short staff policy and training
scenarios.best_way: Allow the approved AI, block the rest by application category, DLP on prompts, and a monthly report.

scenarios.title: IPS is "breaking the ERP"
scenarios.situation: After enabling an IPS sensor, the ERP application intermittently fails. The customer wants IPS turned off.
scenarios.ask: What do you do?
right_thinking: Find the exact signature in the IPS logs
Check it's a false positive, not a real attack
Narrow exception, not disabling IPS
Tune the sensor to the ERP's platform
scenarios.what: A precise exception and a tuned sensor.
scenarios.why: Turning IPS off removes protection for everything else.
how: Filter IPS logs by ERP server IPs
Validate with the vendor or packet capture
Override that signature for those hosts; tune filters
scenarios.model_answer: I'd ask for a bit of time before turning anything off. The IPS logs will show the exact signature, source and destination when the ERP fails. If it's a false positive, I'd add an override for that one signature on the ERP policy, rather than disabling IPS. I'd also tune the sensor to the ERP's platform so it only uses relevant signatures. Then we retest with the ERP team and document the exception.
scenarios.best_way: Find the exact signature in the logs, override just that one if it's a false positive, and tune the sensor.

scenarios.title: What if the customer wants proxy mode everywhere "for maximum security"?
scenarios.situation: A customer on a mid-range model asks for proxy inspection on every policy.
scenarios.ask: What's your recommendation?
right_thinking: Flow is the default and recommended unless a proxy feature is needed
Proxy costs resources and buffering latency
Use proxy where a proxy-only feature is required
scenarios.what: A justified per-policy mode choice.
scenarios.why: Unneeded proxy mode can hurt performance without adding protection.
how: List required proxy-only features per policy
scenarios.model_answer: Proxy isn't automatically more secure; it adds specific features like CDR, WAF, inline CASB and video filter. Fortinet recommends flow unless you need those. I'd list which policies actually need a proxy feature, use proxy only there, and keep the rest flow, which uses fewer resources. If they need proxy broadly, we check the model's sizing first.
scenarios.best_way: Flow by default; proxy only where a proxy-only feature is needed, after checking sizing.

interview.question: Flow versus proxy inspection: when do you use each?
interview.model_answer: "Flow inspects packets as they pass, holding only the last packet until there's a verdict, so it's fast and is the default. Proxy buffers the whole file or page, inspects it, then releases it or shows a replacement message. I use flow unless I need a proxy-only feature like WAF, CDR, inline CASB or video filtering, and I try to keep modes consistent for performance."
interview.best_way: Flow by default; proxy when a proxy-only feature is needed.

interview.question: How would you design an IPS sensor for a DMZ web server?
interview.model_answer: "Tune it to what it protects: server-side signatures filtered by the server's OS and application, say Linux and Apache, blocking critical and high, and default action for medium. Add botnet C&C blocking. Then I review the logs for false positives and adjust with signature overrides, not by turning IPS off."
interview.best_way: Server-side signatures for that OS and app, block high and critical, botnet blocking, then tune from logs.

interview.question: In what order does FortiGate apply web filtering?
interview.model_answer: "URL filter first, then FortiGuard categories, then the content filter, the script filter, and finally antivirus scanning. That's why an exempt in the URL filter is powerful: it skips the later checks."
interview.best_way: URL filter, FortiGuard categories, content, script, then AV.

interview.question: A customer asks how to control generative AI use. What do you propose?
interview.model_answer: "Three layers on FortiGate: web filter with the AI Technology category, application control with the Generative AI category, and DLP on prompts for sensitive data, with deep inspection where needed. Allow the sanctioned tool, measure the rest, then block with evidence. I did this kind of shadow-AI work at Netskope, and visibility first is what made it stick."
interview.best_way: Web filter category, app control, DLP on prompts: allow the sanctioned tool and measure the rest.

interview.question: How do you balance security and usability when deploying controls for a customer?
interview.framework: Monitor → evidence → block → exceptions with owners
interview.model_answer: "I start in monitor mode, so the customer sees what's really happening, and we decide what to block using that evidence. Then we block in phases, with a clear path for exceptions that have an owner and a review date. That way security goes up without surprising the business, and the controls stay switched on."
interview.best_way: Monitor first, block with evidence, exceptions with owners.

field_reports.title: Shadow AI is mainstream
field_reports.body: **45 %** of employees are regular AI users on corporate devices, and shadow AI became the third most common non-malicious insider action in DLP data (2026 DBIR). GenAI controls are now a standard customer request.
field_reports.source: Verizon 2026 DBIR

field_reports.title: AI on the attacker's side too
field_reports.body: IBM's 2026 report saw AI-driven attacks rise **56 %**, adding about **USD 1 million** per breach, while organizations using security AI and automation extensively saved **USD 1.93 million** and **65 days**. FortiGuard's AI-driven signatures and categories are part of that defensive side.
field_reports.source: IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026
